subject: Communication
title: Lost in Translation: Untranslatable Words
description: A 60-second lesson on Lost in Translation: Untranslatable Words.

hook.text: Japanese has 'komorebi' — sunlight filtering through leaves. English has no word for it. Does that mean we don't see it?

buildup.text: Every language has words with no direct translation. 'Saudade' (Portuguese), 'Hygge' (Danish), 'Schadenfreude' (German).

discovery.text: Untranslatable words reveal what a culture pays attention to — and what it finds important enough to name.

twist.text: When you learn a new language, you don't just gain words. You gain new categories of perception and feeling.

climax.text: Cross-cultural communication fails when we assume our language maps perfectly onto another. It never does.

punchline.text: Some feelings only exist in certain languages.

quiz.question: What does the existence of untranslatable words reveal?
options: What a culture pays attention to

details.summary: Many languages contain words that have no direct equivalent in English. Japanese ikigai captures life purpose, Danish hygge embodies cozy togetherness, and Portuguese saudade describes a nostalgic longing. These words reveal cultural values invisible in other languages.
details.whyItMatters: Untranslatable words are windows into cultural values. They reveal what a culture considers important enough to name with a single word.
takeaways: Untranslatable words reveal deep cultural values
They highlight concepts other cultures lack names for
Learning them expands your emotional and cultural vocabulary

faq.question: Can untranslatable words actually be explained in English?
faq.answer: They can be described but not captured in a single word. The descriptions are approximations that lack the cultural weight and emotional resonance of the original. Using the original word in its cultural context conveys meaning that explanation cannot fully deliver.

faq.question: Why do some cultures have words others do not?
faq.answer: Languages develop vocabulary for experiences a culture frequently encounters and values. Inuit languages have many words for snow because distinctions matter for survival. Similarly, Japanese has nuanced vocabulary for social obligation because those distinctions are culturally central.
